The paper concluded people's emotional responses to fiction are irrational.{{sfn|Radford|Weston|1975}} American philosopher [[Kendall Walton]]'s paper "Fearing Fictions" (1978) addresses the paradox.{{sfn|Walton|1978}}{{sfn|Konrad|Petraschka|Werner|2018}} This paper served as the impetus for [[Kendall Walton#Make-believe theory|make-believe theory]].

== Philosophy of language ==
Philosophy of language is still strongly influenced by earlier authors.

=== Semantics===
John Searle advocated Russell's descriptivism and tried to elaborate it with a "cluster theory" of descriptions.<ref name="Stanford">{{cite book|chapter-url=http://plato.stanford.edu/entries/names/#2.1|title=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Names|chapter=Names|year=2019|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University}}</ref> Kripke challenged the descriptivist theory with a [[causal theory of reference]] in ''Naming and Necessity''.{{sfn|Kripke|1980}} According to one author, "In the philosophy of language, ''Naming and Necessity'' is among the most important works ever."{{sfn|Soames|2005|p=336}} Ruth Barcan Marcus also challenged descriptivism with a [[direct reference theory]], in her case a [[tag theory of names]].{{sfn|Marcus|1961}} [[Keith Donnellan]] too challenged descriptivism.{{sfn|Donnellan|1966}}

Hilary Putnam used the Twin Earth and [[brain in a vat]] thought experiments to argue for [[semantic externalism]], or the view that the meanings of words are not psychological.{{sfn|Putnam|1973}}{{sfn|Putnam|1975}}{{sfn|Putnam|1981}} [[Donald Davidson (philosopher)|Donald Davidson]] uses the thought experiment of [[Swampman]] to advocate for semantic externalism.{{sfn|Davidson|1987}} [[Tyler Burge]] uses the thought experiment of [[arthritis]] in one's thigh.{{sfn|Burge|1979}}

Kripke in ''[[Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language]]'' (1982) provides a skeptical, rule-following paradox, undermining the possibility of our ever following rules, and so calls into question the idea of meaning. Kripke writes this paradox is "the most radical and original skeptical problem that philosophy has seen to date".{{sfn|Kripke|1982|p=60}} The [[portmanteau]] "Kripkenstein" has been coined as a term for a fictional person who holds the views expressed by Kripke's reading of Wittgenstein.

[[Alonzo Church]] pioneered intensional logic.<ref name=":2">{{cite SEP|title=Intensional logic}}</ref> Czech philosopher [[Pavel Tichý]] developed [[transparent intensional logic]].<ref name=":2" />

=== Pragmatics ===
[[Paul Grice]] and his [[Grice's maxims|maxims]] and theory of [[implicature]] established the discipline of [[pragmatics]].{{sfn|Grice|1975}} Austin and [[John Searle]] also influenced the field. Pragmatics focuses on [[deixis]] and presuppositions and other context-dependent features of language.{{sfn|Morgan|1977}}{{sfn|Taavitsainen|Jucker|2010}}<ref>{{Citation |last1=Korta |first1=Kepa |title=Pragmatics |date=2024 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2024/entries/pragmatics/ |access-date=2025-06-07 |edition=Fall 2024 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Perry |first2=John |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>

== Philosophy of mind  ==
[[File:John searle2.jpg|thumb|200px|John Searle]]
Analytic philosophy's interest in philosophy of language has arguably been superseded by an interest in the philosophy of mind.{{sfn|Zahavi|2016}} Two common notions in analytic philosophy of mind are intentionality, as above, and [[qualia]], a term introduced by C. I. Lewis.{{sfn|Lewis|1956|p=121}}

=== Physicalism ===
[[Emergent materialism]] holds that mental properties emerge as novel properties of complex material systems.{{sfn|Martinich|Sosa|2001|p=65}} It can be divided into emergence which denies [[mental causation]] and emergence which allows for causal effect.  A version of the latter type was advocated by John Searle, called [[biological naturalism]].{{efn|Searle famously [[Searle-Derrida debate|debated]] continental philosopher [[Jacques Derrida|Derrida]].{{sfn|Alfino|1991}}}}  [[Douglas Hofstadter]] also believes the mind is emergent in ''[[Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid]]'', from [[self-reference|self-referential]] "[[strange loops]]".{{sfn|Hofstadter|1979}}

The other main group of materialist views in the philosophy of mind can be labeled non-emergent (or non-emergentist) materialism, and includes philosophical [[logical behaviorism|behaviorism]], [[type-token distinction|type]] [[Identity theory of mind|identity theory]] (reductive materialism), [[Functionalism (philosophy of mind)|functionalism]], and pure physicalism ([[eliminative materialism]]).

==== Behaviorism ====
{{see also|Verbal Behavior#Chomsky's review and replies}}
Motivated by the logical positivists, behaviorism was the most prominent theory of mind in analytic philosophy for the first half of the twentieth century.{{sfn|Geach|1957}} Behaviorists believed either that statements about the mind were equivalent to ''statements about'' behavior and [[disposition]]s to behave in particular ways; or that mental states were directly equivalent to behavior and dispositions to behave. Hilary Putnam criticized behaviorism by arguing that it confuses the symptoms of mental states with the mental states themselves, positing "super Spartans" who never display signs of pain.{{sfn|Putnam|1965}}
 
[[File:Hilary Putnam.jpg|thumb|200px|Hilary Putnam]]

==== Type identity ====
Behaviorism later became much less popular in favor of either type identity theory or functionalism.<ref>{{cite SEP|title=Consciousness}}</ref> Type identity theory or type physicalism identified mental states with brain states. Former students of Ryle at the [[University of Adelaide]]  [[J. J. C. Smart|Jack Smart]] and [[Ullin Place]] argued for type physicalism.{{sfn|Smart|1959}}{{sfn|Place|1956}} Type identity was criticized by Putnam and others using [[multiple realizability]].{{sfn|Putnam|1960}} The criticism spawned [[anomalous monism]].{{sfn|Davidson|1970}}

==== Functionalism ====
Functionalism remains the dominant theory.{{efn|In a 2020 [[PhilPapers]] survey, 33% of respondents were accepting or leaning towards it.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020 |title=Survey Results {{!}} Consciousness: panpsychism, dualism, eliminativism, functionalism, or identity theory? |url=https://survey2020.philpeople.org/survey/results/5010? |website=PhilPapers}}</ref>}} [[Computational theory of mind|Computationalism]] is a kind of functionalism. The view was first associated with Sellars.{{sfn|Dennett|1989|p=341}} Putnam was also a functionalist.{{sfn|Putnam|1960}}  Another functionalist was [[Jerry Fodor]], who is known for proposing the [[modularity of mind]], a theory of [[Psychological nativism|innateness]].{{sfn|Fodor|1983}} He also introduced the [[language of thought hypothesis]], which describes thought as possessing syntax or compositional structure (sometimes known as mentalese).{{sfn|Fodor|1975}} Searle's [[Chinese room]] argument criticized functionalism and holds that while a computer can understand syntax, it could never understand semantics.{{sfn|Searle|1980}} A similar idea is [[Ned Block]]'s [[China brain]].{{sfn|Block|1978}}

==== Eliminativism ====
The view of eliminative materialism is most closely associated with [[Paul Churchland|Paul]] and [[Patricia Churchland]], who deny the existence of propositional attitudes;{{sfn|Churchland|1981}} and with [[Daniel Dennett]], who in works like ''[[Consciousness Explained]]'' (1991) is generally considered an eliminativist about qualia and phenomenal aspects of consciousness (but not about [[intentional stance|intentionality]]{{sfn|Dennett|1989}}).{{sfn|Dennett|1988}}{{sfn|Dennett|1991}} Dennett coined the term "[[intuition pump]]."{{sfn|Dennett|1984|p=12}} Thomas Nagel's paper "[[What Is It Like to Be a Bat?]]" challenged the physicalist account of mind;{{sfn|Nagel|1974}} so did [[Frank Jackson (philosopher)|Frank Jackson]]'s [[knowledge argument]], which argues for qualia.{{sfn|Jackson|1982}}{{sfn|Jackson|1986}}

=== Dualism ===
[[File:David chalmers.jpg|thumb|David Chalmers]]

Finally, analytic philosophy has featured a certain number of philosophers who were dualists, and recently forms of [[property dualism]] have had a resurgence; the most prominent representative is [[David Chalmers]].<ref>{{cite SEP|url-id=dualism|title=Dualism}}</ref> Chalmers introduced the notion of the [[hard problem of consciousness]]. He has criticized [[Interactionism (philosophy of mind)|interactionism]] and shown sympathy with [[neutral monism]]. Kripke also makes a notable argument for dualism.{{sfn|Kripke|1980|pp=145–146}}{{sfn|Jacquette|1987}} [[Epiphenomenalism]], the view that mental events are caused by physical events in the brain but do not cause anything else in return, is sometimes classed as a kind of property dualism.{{sfn|Jackson|1982}}{{sfn|Bacrac|2010}}

=== Panpsychism ===
Yet another view is [[panpsychism]], or the view that mentality is fundamental and ubiquitous in the natural world.{{sfn|Nagel|1979}} Panpsychism can be contrasted with [[idealism]] by still believing in matter.{{efn|While analytic idealism remains a minority position, one notable example is the work of [[Bernardo Kastrup]].{{sfn|Kastrup|2019}} It seeks to resolve the so-called hard problem of consciousness by taking experience as ontologically fundamental.{{sfn|Kastrup|2019}}}}

=== Perception and consciousness ===
In recent years, a central focus of research in the philosophy of mind has been consciousness and the philosophy of perception. The [[homunculus argument]] is an objection raised against many older theories of perception.{{sfn|Dennett|1996b}}  While there is now a general consensus for the global neuronal workspace model of consciousness,{{sfn|Dennett|2001}} there are many opinions as to the specifics. The best known theories in analytic philosophy are Searle's naive realism, Fred Dretske and [[Michael Tye (philosopher)|Michael Tye]]'s [[direct and indirect realism|representationalism]], Dennett's [[heterophenomenology]], and the [[Higher-order theories of consciousness|higher-order theories]] of either [[David M. Rosenthal (philosopher)|David M. Rosenthal]]—who advocates a higher-order thought (HOT) model—or David Armstrong and [[William Lycan]]—who advocate a higher-order perception (HOP) model.{{sfn|Van Gulick|2006}}{{efn|An alternative higher-order theory, the higher-order global states (HOGS) model, is offered by [[Robert van Gulick]].{{sfn|Van Gulick|2004}}}}

== Philosophy of mathematics ==
[[File:Kurt gödel.jpg|thumb|200px|Kurt Gödel]]

[[Kurt Gödel]], a student of Hans Hahn of the Vienna Circle, produced his [[Gödel's incompleteness theorems|incompleteness theorems]] showing that ''Principia Mathematica'' also failed to reduce arithmetic to logic, and that [[Hilbert's program]] was unattainable.{{sfn|Gödel|1931}} [[Ernst Zermelo]] and [[Abraham Fraenkel]] established [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|Zermelo Fraenkel Set Theory]] (with the [[axiom of choice]], abbreviated as ZFC).<ref name=":0" /> Quine developed his own system, dubbed [[New Foundations]].{{sfn|Quine|1953}}

Physicist [[Eugene Wigner]]'s seminal paper "[[The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences]]" (1960) poses the question of why a formal pursuit like mathematics can have real utility.{{sfn|Wigner|1960}}

[[Hilbert's Hotel]] shows some of the counterintuitive properties of [[infinite set]]s.{{sfn|Gamow|2012|p=17}} [[José Benardete]] in ''Infinity: An Essay in Metaphysics'' (1964) argued for the reality of [[infinity]].{{sfn|Benardete|1964}} The [[Grim Reaper paradox]] stems from his work.{{sfn|Koons|2014}} [[Finitism|Finitists]] reject infinity.<ref name=":0" />

Akin to the medieval debate on universals, between realists, idealists, and nominalists; the philosophy of mathematics has the debate between logicists or platonists, conceptualists or [[Intuitionism|intuitionists]], and [[Formalism (philosophy of mathematics)|formalists]].{{sfn|Quine|1948}}

=== Platonism ===
Gödel was a platonist who postulated a special kind of intuition that lets one perceive mathematical objects directly.{{sfn|Parsons|1995}} Quine and Putnam argued for platonism with the [[Quine–Putnam indispensability argument|indispensability argument]].<ref name=":0"/>  [[Edward N. Zalta|Edward Zalta]] devised [[Abstract and concrete|abstract object]] [[Abstract object theory|theory]].{{sfn|Zalta|1983}} [[Crispin Wright]], along with [[Bob Hale (philosopher)|Bob Hale]], led a Neo-Fregean revival with the work ''Frege's Conception of Numbers as Objects'' (1983).{{sfn|Wright|1983}} Physicist [[Roger Penrose]] is also a mathematical platonist, in works like ''[[The Road to Reality]]'' (2004).{{sfn|Penrose|2007|p=15}}

[[Structuralism (philosophy of mathematics)|Structuralist]] [[Paul Benacerraf]] has two well-known objections to mathematical platonism; one is about [[Benacerraf's identification problem|identification]],{{sfn|Benacerraf|1965}} and the other [[Benacerraf's epistemological problem|epistemological]].{{sfn|Benacerraf|1973}} In the latter, Benacerraf argues that while platonism explains mathematical semantics, it does not simultaneously explain mathematical knowledge. It is hard to know anything about a far-removed, platonic object.{{sfn|Benacerraf|1973}} [[Impredicativity|Predicativism]] is another alternative to platonism, utilizing [[Henri Poincaré]]'s response to Russell's paradox.<ref name=":0">{{cite SEP|title=Philosophy of Mathematics}}</ref> There are also [[Aristotelian realist philosophy of mathematics|Aristotelians]] in mathematics, such as [[Dale Jacquette]].{{sfn|Jacquette|2014}}

=== Intuitionism ===
The intuitionists, led by Dutch mathematician [[L. E. J. Brouwer]], are a [[Constructivism (philosophy of mathematics)|constructivist]] school which sees mathematics as a [[Cognition|cognitive]] [[Construct (philosophy)|construct]] rather than a type of [[objective truth]].<ref name=":0" /> Brouwer also influenced Wittgenstein's abandonment of the ''Tractatus''.{{sfn|Monk|1990|page= 250}}

=== Formalism ===
The formalists, best exemplified by David Hilbert, considered mathematics to be merely the investigation of [[Formal system|formal axiom systems]].<ref name=":0" /> [[Hartry Field]] defended [[mathematical fictionalism]] in ''[[Science Without Numbers]]'' (1980), arguing numbers are dispensable.{{sfn|Field|2016}}

== Philosophy of religion ==
In ''Analytic Philosophy of Religion'', [[James Franklin Harris]] noted that:

{{blockquote|
...analytic philosophy has been a very heterogeneous 'movement'.... some forms of analytic philosophy have proven very sympathetic to the philosophy of religion and have provided a philosophical mechanism for responding to other more radical and hostile forms of analytic philosophy.{{sfn|Harris|2002|p=3}}}}

Analytic philosophy tended to avoid the study of [[Philosophy of religion|religion]], largely dismissing (as per the logical positivists) the subject as a part of metaphysics and therefore meaningless.{{efn|A notable exception is the series of [[Michael Foster (philosopher)|Michael B. Foster]]'s 1934–36 ''Mind'' articles involving the Christian doctrine of creation and the rise of modern science.{{sfn|Foster|1934}}{{sfn|Foster|1935}}{{sfn|Foster|1936}}}} The demise of logical positivism led to a renewed interest in the philosophy of religion, prompting philosophers not only to introduce new problems, but to re-study perennial topics such as the [[existence of God]], the rationality of belief, the nature of [[miracle]]s, the [[problem of evil]], and several others.{{sfn|Peterson|1991}} The [[Society of Christian Philosophers]] was established in 1978.

=== Reformed epistemology ===
Analytic philosophy formed the basis for some sophisticated Christian arguments, such as those of the [[reformed epistemology|reformed epistemologists]] including [[Alvin Plantinga]], [[William Alston]], and [[Nicholas Wolterstorff]].

[[File:AlvinPlantinga.JPG|thumb|200px|Alvin Plantinga]]

Plantinga was once described by ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine as "America's leading orthodox [[Protestantism|Protestant]] philosopher of God".<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/archive/6855863/religion-modernizing-the-case-for-god/|title=Religion: Modernizing the Case for God|date=April 7, 1980|magazine=Time}}</ref> His seminal work ''[[God and Other Minds]]'' (1967) argues belief in God is a properly [[basic belief]] akin to the belief in other minds.{{sfn|Plantinga|1967}} Plantinga also developed a modal [[Ontological argument#Alvin Plantinga|ontological argument]] in ''The Nature of Necessity'' (1974).{{sfn|Plantinga|1974}} Plantinga, John Mackie, and [[Antony Flew]] debated the use of the ''[[Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense|free will defense]]'' as a way to solve the problem of evil.{{sfn|Mackie|1982}} Plantinga further issued a trilogy on epistemology, ''[[Warrant: The Current Debate]]'' (1993), ''[[Warrant and Proper Function]]'' (1993), and ''[[Warranted Christian Belief]]'' (2000).{{sfn|Plantinga|1993a}}{{sfn|Plantinga|1993b}}{{sfn|Plantinga|2000}} Plantinga's [[evolutionary argument against naturalism]] contends there is a problem in asserting both evolution and naturalism.{{sfn|Plantinga|1993b|p=235}}

Alston defended [[divine command theory]].{{sfn|Alston|1990}} [[Robert Merrihew Adams]] also defended divine command theory, and the virtue of [[faith]].{{sfn|Adams|1987}} [[William Lane Craig]] defends the [[Kalam cosmological argument]] in the [[The Kalām Cosmological Argument|book]] of the same name.{{sfn|Craig|1979}}

=== Analytic Thomism ===
Catholic analytic philosophers—such as Elizabeth Anscombe, her husband [[Peter Geach]], MacIntyre, [[Anthony Kenny]], [[John Haldane (philosopher)|John Haldane]], [[Eleonore Stump]], and others—developed [[Analytical Thomism|Analytic]] [[Thomism]].{{sfn|Anscombe|Geach|1961}}{{sfn|Haldane|2004}}

=== Eastern Orthodoxy ===
Eastern Orthodox convert [[Richard Swinburne]] wrote a trilogy of books arguing for God,  ''The Coherence of Theism'' (1977), ''[[The Existence of God (book)|The Existence of God]]'' (1979), and ''Faith and Reason'' (1981).{{sfn|Swinburne|1977}}{{sfn|Swinburne|2004}}{{sfn|Swinburne|1981}} Swinburne is notable for his belief that God's existence is contingent rather than necessary (it is possible God does not exist), but that nonetheless He does exist as a [[brute fact]].{{sfn|Leftow|2010}}

=== Wittgenstein and religion ===
The analytic philosophy of religion has been preoccupied with Wittgenstein, as well as his interpretation of [[Søren Kierkegaard]].{{sfn|Creegan|1989}} Wittgenstein fought for the Austrian army in [[World War I]] and came upon a copy of Leo Tolstoy's ''[[The Gospel in Brief]]'' (1896). He subsequently underwent some kind of religious conversion.{{sfn|Monk|1990|p=115}}{{sfn|Schardt|Large|2001}} "[[Swansea University|Swansea]] school" philosophers such as Rush Rhees, [[Peter Winch]], and [[D. Z. Phillips]], among others, founded a school of religious thought based on Wittgenstein. The name "contemplative philosophy" was coined by Phillips in ''Philosophy's Cool Place'' (1999),{{efn|This interpretation was first labeled "Wittgensteinian [[Fideism]]" by [[Kai Nielsen (philosopher)|Kai Nielsen]], but those who consider themselves members of the Swansea school rejected this construal as a caricature of Wittgenstein's position; this is especially true of Phillips.<ref>{{cite SEP|url-id=fideism|title=Fideism}}</ref> Nielsen and Phillips subsequently became two of the most prominent interpreters of Wittgenstein's philosophy of religion.{{sfn|Nielsen|Phillips|2005}}}} after a passage quoted in Wittgenstein's ''[[Culture and Value]]'' (1980).{{sfn|Phillips|1999}}{{efn|"My ideal is a certain coolness. A temple providing a setting for the passions without meddling with them."{{sfn|Wittgenstein|1984|loc=2e}}}}

== Philosophy of science ==
The weight given to scientific evidence is largely due to philosophers' commitments to [[scientific realism]] and [[Naturalism (philosophy)|naturalism]]. Some such as [[Friedrich Hayek]] in ''[[The Counter-Revolution of Science]]'' (1952) see using science in philosophy as [[scientism]].{{sfn|Hayek|1952}} Nonetheless, science has had an increasingly significant role in analytic philosophy. The theory of special relativity has had a profound effect on the philosophy of time,{{sfn|van Inwagen|Zimmerman|1991|p=163}} and [[quantum physics]] is routinely discussed in the free will debate.{{sfn|van Inwagen|Zimmerman|1991|p=318}} [[Ernest Nagel]]'s book ''[[The Structure of Science]]'' (1961) practically inaugurated the field of philosophy of science.{{sfn|Nagel|1961}}

=== Theories ===

Carl Hempel advocated confirmation theory or [[Bayesian epistemology]]. He introduced the famous [[Raven paradox|raven's paradox]].{{sfn|Fitelson|Hawthorne|2010}}
[[File:Karl Popper.jpg|thumb|200px|Karl Popper]]

In reaction to what he considered excesses of logical positivism, Karl Popper, in ''[[The Logic of Scientific Discovery]]'' (1959), rejects the standard [[inductivist]] views on the [[scientific method]] in favor of a highly influential theory of [[falsifiability|falsification]], using it to solve the [[demarcation problem]].{{sfn|Popper|2002}}

Quine and French scientist [[Pierre Duhem]] seemed to have similar views in certain respects. The [[Duhem–Quine thesis]], or problem of [[underdetermination]], posits that no [[Hypothesis|scientific hypothesis]] can be understood in isolation, a viewpoint called [[confirmation holism]].{{sfn|Quine|1951}} Following Quine and Duhem, subsequent theories emphasized [[theory-ladenness]].

In reaction to both the logical positivists and Popper, philosophy became dominated by [[social constructivism|social constructivist]] and [[cognitive relativism|cognitive relativist]] theories of science. Significant for these discussions is [[Thomas Samuel Kuhn|Thomas Kuhn]], who in ''[[The Structure of Scientific Revolutions]]'' (1962) formulated the idea of [[paradigm shift]]s and sparked a "revolt against positivism" known as the "[[historicist|historical]]  turn".{{sfn|Kuhn|1962}}{{sfn|Glock|2008|page=47}} [[Paul Feyerabend]]'s book ''[[Against Method]]'' (1975) advocates [[epistemological anarchism]]; that there are no universal rules for scientific inquiry.{{sfn|Feyerabend|1975}}

=== Branches ===
Philosophers like [[Tim Maudlin]] focus on the [[philosophy of physics]]. Maudlin argues in ''The Metaphysics Within Physics'' (2007) that philosophy must reflect on physics, and that [[scientific laws]] are ''sui generis''.{{sfn|Maudlin|2007}} Recently there has also been work in the [[philosophy of chemistry]],{{sfn|van Brakel|2000}} and the [[philosophy of biology]] has undergone considerable growth, especially due to the debate over the nature of [[evolution]], particularly [[natural selection]].{{sfn|Hull|Ruse|2007|p=xix, xx}} Daniel Dennett and his book ''[[Darwin's Dangerous Idea]]'' (1995), which defends [[Neo-Darwinism]], stand at the forefront of this debate.{{sfn|Dennett|1996a}}{{sfn|Lennox|2008|p=89}} Jerry Fodor criticizes natural selection in ''[[What Darwin Got Wrong]]'' (2010).{{sfn|Fodor|Piattelli-Palmarini|2010}}

The [[philosophy of social science]] has also received increased interest. Peter Winch takes a Wittgensteinian perspective in ''The Idea of a Social Science and its Relation to Philosophy'' (1958).{{sfn|Winch|2002}} Searle contributed to [[social ontology]] and the theory of [[social constructs]] with ''The Construction of Social Reality'' (1995).{{sfn|Searle|1995}}
